preamble.summary: The chapter opens with beatitudes for the person whose mouth has not betrayed him and whose conscience does not condemn him. It then warns against miserliness: the miser harms himself, hoarding wealth he will never enjoy. Ben Sira counsels enjoying God's good gifts before death, since in Sheol there is no pleasure. The chapter concludes with a beautiful passage on the pursuit of wisdom: blessed is the one who camps near her house and pitches his tent beside her walls.
preamble.remarkable: The carpe diem passage (vv. 11-19) is the most Epicurean-sounding text in the deuterocanonical literature. Ben Sira, who elsewhere warns against luxury, here urges enjoyment of God's gifts. This tension reflects the wisdom tradition's refusal to be systematized: neither asceticism nor indulgence, but appropriate enjoyment within divine boundaries. The closing wisdom-pursuit passage (vv. 20-27) is among the most lyrical in the book.
preamble.friction: The view of death as final (vv. 16-17) -- with no hope of resurrection or afterlife pleasure -- represents a pre-resurrection theology. Sheol is simply the place of ending. This stands in tension with Daniel 12:2 and 2 Maccabees 7, which were developing resurrection theology in the same period.
preamble.connections: Ecclesiastes 9:7-10 (eat, drink, and enjoy, for there is no work in Sheol); Psalm 1:1-3 (blessed is the one who meditates on Torah); Proverbs 8:34-35 (blessed is the one who watches at wisdom's gates); Isaiah 40:6-8 (all flesh is grass); Luke 12:19-20 (eat, drink, be merry -- but this night your soul is required).

verses.text_latin: Beatus vir qui non est lapsus verbo ex ore suo et non est stimulatus in tristitia delicti.
verses.rendering: Blessed is the man who has not slipped with a word from his mouth, and is not stung by the grief of sin.
translator_notes: A beatitude for moral integrity in speech and conscience. The word 'stimulatus' (stung) suggests the ongoing pain of a guilty conscience.

key_terms.note: The classic biblical macarism; beatus declares a state of flourishing under God's favor.

verses.text_latin: Felix qui non habuit animi sui tristitiam et non excidit a spe sua.
verses.rendering: Happy is the one whose spirit has no cause for sorrow, and who has not fallen from his hope.
translator_notes: Felix complements beatus: the person free of self-reproach and still sustained by hope.

verses.text_latin: Viro cupido et tenaci sine ratione est substantia et homini livido ad quid aurum.
verses.rendering: For a greedy and grasping man, wealth has no purpose; and for an envious person, what good is gold?
translator_notes: Wealth without generosity is meaningless; the miser possesses but cannot enjoy.

key_terms.note: A double characterization: cupidus (desiring) and tenax (clutching); the miser both craves and clings.

verses.text_latin: Qui acervat ex animo suo iniuste aliis congregat et in bonis illius alius luxuriabitur.
verses.rendering: Whoever hoards unjustly from his own soul gathers for others, and another will revel in his goods.
translator_notes: The miser's irony: he deprives himself and enriches his heirs.

verses.text_latin: Qui sibi nequam est cui alii bonus erit et non iucundabitur in bonis suis.
verses.rendering: Whoever is evil to himself, to whom will he be good? He will take no pleasure in his own possessions.
translator_notes: A penetrating question: self-deprivation through miserliness is a form of self-harm.

verses.text_latin: Qui sibi invidet nihil est illo nequius et haec redditio est malitiae illius.
verses.rendering: There is no one more wretched than the one who begrudges himself, and this is the repayment for his wickedness.

verses.text_latin: Et si bene fecerit ignoranter et non volens facit et in novissimo manifestat malitiam suam.
verses.rendering: And if he does good, he does it unknowingly and unwillingly, and in the end he reveals his true malice.

verses.text_latin: Nequam est oculus lividi et avertens faciem suam et despiciens animam suam.
verses.rendering: Evil is the eye of the envious; he turns away his face and despises his own soul.
translator_notes: The 'evil eye' (oculus nequam) in the Semitic tradition represents stinginess and envy -- the refusal to look generously on others.

key_terms.note: The evil eye tradition: an envious gaze that wishes harm or withholds good.

verses.text_latin: Insatiabilis oculus cupidi in parte iniquitatis non satiabitur donec consumat arefaciens animam suam.
verses.rendering: The eye of the greedy is not satisfied with his share of iniquity; he will not be sated until he has shriveled his own soul.
translator_notes: Greed is self-consuming: the soul withers (arefaciens) even as the possessions accumulate.

verses.text_latin: Oculus malus ad mala et non satiabitur pane sed indigens et in tristitia erit super mensam suam.
verses.rendering: An evil eye begrudges even bread; he is needy and sorrowful at his own table.
translator_notes: The miser sits at a table laden with food but experiences deprivation -- a psychological poverty amid material abundance.

verses.text_latin: Fili si habes benefac tecum et Deo dignas oblationes offer.
verses.rendering: My son, if you have means, treat yourself well, and offer worthy oblations to God.
translator_notes: The pivot to enjoyment: generosity toward self and toward God are both commanded. Neither miserliness nor impiety is acceptable.

verses.text_latin: Memor esto quoniam mors non tardat et testamentum inferorum quod demonstratum est tibi testamentum enim huius mundi morte morietur.
verses.rendering: Remember that death does not delay, and the decree of the grave has been shown to you; for the covenant of this world is death -- it will surely die.
translator_notes: The memento mori intensifies: death is not a distant possibility but an approaching certainty. The 'covenant of this world' is mortality itself.

key_terms.note: Testamentum here means an established ordinance or decree; death is the fixed decree governing all flesh.

verses.text_latin: Ante mortem benefac amico tuo et secundum vires tuas exporrigens da pauperi.
verses.rendering: Before death, do good to your friend, and according to your ability reach out and give to the poor.
translator_notes: The urgency of generosity: once dead, you can neither give nor receive.

verses.text_latin: Non defrauderis a die bono et particula boni doni non te praetereat.
verses.rendering: Do not let a good day pass you by, and do not let your share of a good gift escape you.
translator_notes: Carpe diem theology: enjoy what God gives while you can.

verses.text_latin: Nonne aliis relinques dolores et labores tuos et in divisione sortis.
verses.rendering: Will you not leave your griefs and labors to others, and your toil to be divided by lot?
translator_notes: Everything accumulated will pass to heirs who may squander or divide it; the hoarder's labor benefits others, not himself.

verses.text_latin: Da et accipe et iustifica animam tuam.
verses.rendering: Give and receive, and treat your soul justly.
translator_notes: A concise summary of balanced living: generosity, enjoyment, and self-care.

verses.text_latin: Ante obitum tuum operare iustitiam quoniam non est apud inferos invenire cibum.
verses.rendering: Before your death, work righteousness, for in the realm of the dead there is no finding of food.
translator_notes: Sheol offers nothing; all opportunity for righteous action ends at death.

key_terms.note: Inferi/Sheol is the shadowy underworld where the dead exist without activity or pleasure.

verses.text_latin: Omnis caro sicut faenum veterascet et sicut folium fructificans in arbore viridi.
verses.rendering: All flesh ages like grass, and like a leaf that grows green on a flourishing tree.
translator_notes: The grass metaphor for mortality is shared with Isaiah 40:6-8 and Psalm 103:15-16.

verses.text_latin: Alia generantur et alia deiciuntur sic generatio carnis et sanguinis alia finitur et alia nascitur.
verses.rendering: Some leaves sprout and others fall; so it is with generations of flesh and blood -- one comes to an end, and another is born.
translator_notes: The cycle of generations mirrors the cycle of leaves: perpetual replacement, individual impermanence.

verses.text_latin: Omne opus corruptibile in fine deficiet et qui illud operatur ibit cum illo.
verses.rendering: Every corruptible work will fail in the end, and the one who made it will go with it.
translator_notes: Human works share human mortality; only what transcends corruption endures.

verses.text_latin: Et omne opus electum iustificabitur et qui operatur illud honorabitur in illo.
verses.rendering: But every excellent work will be vindicated, and the one who does it will be honored through it.
translator_notes: The contrast with verse 20: while corruptible works perish, excellent works endure and bring lasting honor.

verses.text_latin: Beatus vir qui in sapientia morabitur et qui in iustitia sua meditabitur et in sensu cogitabit circumspectionem Dei.
verses.rendering: Blessed is the man who dwells in wisdom, and who meditates on her righteousness, and in his mind considers the watchful providence of God.
translator_notes: The second beatitude of the chapter opens the closing wisdom-pursuit section. Dwelling in wisdom means making it one's permanent habitation.

verses.text_latin: Qui excogitat vias illius in corde suo et in absconditis suis intellegens vadens post illam quasi investigator et in viis illius consistens.
verses.rendering: The one who ponders her ways in his heart, and has understanding in her hidden things, who goes after her like a tracker, and stations himself on her paths.
translator_notes: The pursuit of wisdom as a hunt: tracking, following, stationing oneself. The investigator (investigator) is literally one who follows footprints.

key_terms.note: From investigare, to follow tracks; wisdom is quarry to be pursued with the skill and patience of a hunter.

verses.text_latin: Qui respicit per fenestras illius et in ianuis illius audiens.
verses.rendering: The one who peers through her windows, and listens at her doors.
translator_notes: The wisdom-seeker becomes a devoted suitor, looking through windows and listening at doors -- images of longing and attentiveness.

verses.text_latin: Qui requiescit iuxta domum illius et in parietibus illius figens palum statuet casulam suam ad manus illius et requiescent in casula illius bona per aevum.
verses.rendering: The one who rests near her house, and drives a stake in her walls, and pitches his tent at her side -- good things will rest in his tent forever.
translator_notes: The culminating image: the wisdom-seeker camps permanently beside wisdom's house, driving stakes into her very walls. The intimacy is extraordinary -- not occasional visits but permanent encampment.

key_terms.note: Casula is a small dwelling or tent; the seeker builds his life in wisdom's shadow.

verses.text_latin: Statuet filios suos sub tegmine illius et sub ramis eius morabitur.
verses.rendering: He will place his children under her shelter, and will dwell beneath her branches.
translator_notes: Wisdom as a tree providing shade: the seeker's entire family benefits from his choice to camp near her.

verses.text_latin: Protegetur sub tegmine illius a fervore et in gloria eius requiescet.
verses.rendering: He will be sheltered under her covering from the heat, and will rest in her glory.
translator_notes: The chapter ends in rest and glory -- the reward of the one who pursued wisdom with the passion of a hunter and the devotion of a lover.
